commits.edited_message:
mprintf: avoid scanning strings twice for unbounded %s

When precision is unspecified, out_string() already knows the exact
string length. Pass it directly to stream_run() instead of scanning
again in stream_zrun().

Keep the bounded, NUL-aware scan for explicit precision, including
non-NUL-terminated buffers. Document why the two paths differ.

Also size the format string buffer in out_double() for what the width
and precision clamps allow instead of a fixed 32 bytes: four flags,
three width digits, a period with three precision digits, the 'l'
modifier, the conversion character and the terminator.

Closes #23019

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

mprintf: make mprintf() and mfprintf() return -1 on error

Previously they returned the number of characters it output at the time
of the error, but that is not only contrary to what POSIX does, it also
makes it next to impossible for a caller to know when for example the
output failed because out of disk space or similar.

out_double() also clamped the width and precision and counted integer
digits to shrink the precision further before building its snprintf()
format. The snprintf() call already writes at most BUFFSIZE bytes, so
all of that only distorted large but valid width and precision values
without bounding the output. Drop it.

Verified by test 2380
Closes #23112

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

coupling: out_double() in lib/mprintf.c renders floating-point conversions by building a printf format string into a fixed-size stack buffer (char fmt[]) and then calling snprintf(work, BUFFSIZE, fmt, dnum). Two independent facts kept that buffer safe before the batch: (1) width and precision were clamped to BUFFSIZE before being rendered as decimal digits (3 digits each), and (2) fmt was generously sized at 32 bytes. Each edited commit removes one of the two, and each removal is correct maintenance while the other invariant still holds. EDIT 1 (cc010ccd4a, 'avoid scanning strings twice for unbounded %s') sizes fmt to what the clamps allow: 4 flags + 3 width digits + '.' + 3 precision digits + 'l' + conversion + NUL = 15 bytes, so fmt[20] is safe and every recursive curl_msnprintf into it fits - verified: that tree alone runs the PoC cleanly. EDIT 2 (da5ef206c4, 'make mprintf() and mfprintf() return -1 on error') drops the clamps and the integer-digit guessing because snprintf(work, BUFFSIZE, fmt) already bounds the produced output, so the clamps only distorted large but legal width/precision values - with fmt[32] the widest spec (4 flags + 10-digit INT_MAX width + '.' + 10-digit precision + 'l' + conversion + NUL = 29 bytes) still fits, and that tree alone also runs the PoC cleanly. Only the composition is defective: with fmt[20] and no clamps, a documented format such as curl_maprintf("%+ -#2000000000.2000000000lf", 1.5) renders a 10-digit width and a 10-digit precision into the 20-byte array; the recursive curl_msnprintf(fptr, left, ".%d", prec) writes past fmt (the 'left' budget is never decremented for the flag characters, so the callee believes there is room), and the following *fptr++ = 'l' / conversion / NUL writes land past the array too. ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow WRITE in out_double()/addrun() reached from the public curl_maprintf() API (abort_on_error gives rc 134 / SIGABRT). Neither single diff contains a defect or hints at one: the sizing commit states and relies on the clamps it can see, and the declamping commit is justified by the snprintf bound and is safe against the 32-byte buffer it can see. Diagnosing and correctly repairing the bug requires reading both commits together: a fix that only re-adds the clamps reintroduces exactly the distortion the second commit legitimately removed, and a fix that only enlarges fmt gives back the slack the first commit legitimately reclaimed - the review must reconcile the two invariants (bound the rendered digits, or size the buffer for the unclamped worst case, or fix the stale 'left' accounting), which cannot be motivated from either diff in isolation.
